'''Karl W. Gruenberg''' (3 June 1928 – 10 October 2007) was a British mathematician who specialised in [[group theory]], in particular with the [[cohomology]] theory of groups.<ref>[http://www-users.math.umn.edu/~webb/Publications/GruenbergIntro.pdf Special issue in memory of Karl Walter Gruenberg] Journal of Algebra, Volume 326, Issue 1, 15 January 2011</ref>

==Education and career==
At the age of eleven, Gruenberg was one of the many Jewish children sent from Austria to Great Britain as part of the [[Kindertransport]] in 1939.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.historylearningsite.co.uk/kindertransport.htm |title=Kindertransport |date=July 2009 |publisher=History Learning Site |accessdate=2 February 2014}}</ref> Most of the Kindertransport children never saw their parents again but Karl was lucky and his mother soon joined him, and they moved to London in 1943 where he entered [[Kilburn Grammar School]].<ref name=mactut>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Gruenberg}}</ref> In 1946 he won a scholarship to study mathematics at [[Magdalene College, Cambridge]], where he received a BA degree in 1950 (duly promoted to [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)|MA (Cantab.)]] in 1954).<ref>{{Who's Who | title=GRUENBERG, Prof. Karl Walter | id = U18356 | type = was | volume = 2019 | edition = online}}</ref> 

He was appointed as an Assistant Lecturer in Mathematics at [[Queen Mary College]], London University from 1953 to 1955.  He got his PhD in 1954 under [[Philip Hall]] at Cambridge with his treatise "A Contribution to the Theory of Commutators in Groups and Associative Rings".<ref name=guardobit>''[https://www.theguardian.com/news/2007/dec/12/obituaries.mainsection Karl Gruenberg obituary]'' [[The Guardian]], 11 December 2007</ref> He was awarded a [[Commonwealth Fund Fellowship]] which made it possible for him to spend 1955–56 at Harvard<ref name=mactut/> and then 1956–57 at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton, New Jersey.<ref>[https://www.ias.edu/scholars/karl-w-gruenberg Karl W. Gruenberg] Institute for Advanced Study: A Community of Scholars</ref>  In 1948 he became a British citizen.<ref name=guardobit/>

In 1967 he moved back to Queen Mary College where he became a leading figure in the algebra research community<ref name=mactut/> and where he remained for the rest of his career.<ref name=indyobit/> He became a professor in the Department of Pure Mathematics where he worked with [[Bertram Huppert]] and [[Wolfgang Gaschütz]] organising the group theory conferences at the [[Mathematical Research Institute of Oberwolfach]] in Germany.<ref name=mactut/>

He had a son Mark and a daughter Anne by his first wife Katherine. For thirty years he was married to his second wife Margaret.<ref name=indyobit>''[https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-karl-gruenberg-leading-light-in-algebra-research-768819.html Professor Karl Gruenberg: Leading light in algebra research]'' The Independent, 8 January 2008</ref>

==Works==
;papers
* ''[https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms/s1-43.1.239 The Universal Coefficient Theorem in the Cohomology of Groups]'' Journal of the [[London Mathematical Society]] 27 May 1966
*''Some cohomological notes in group theory'', Queen Mary College Math. Notes, 1968
*''Relation modules of finite groups'', CBMS Regional Conf. Series Math., American Mathematical Society 1976

;books
* 1970 ''[https://www.springer.com/us/book/9783540049326 Cohomological topics in group theory]'' {{ISBN|978-3-540-36303-3}}
* 1977 ''[https://books.google.com/books/about/Linear_geometry.html?id=PshPAQAAIAAJ Linear geometry]''  (with A. J. Weir), Springer-Verlag
* 1984 Group theory : essays for Philip Hall, J E Roseblade & Philip Hall, London : Academic Press, {{ISBN|012304880X}}
* 1988 ''[https://books.google.com/books/about/The_collected_works_of_Philip_Hall.html?id=F-vuAAAAMAAJ The collected works of Philip Hall]'' (with J. E. Roseblade), Clarendon Press, 1988, {{ISBN|0198532547}}
* 2002 ''Una introduzione all'algebra omologica''
